  ggplot(aes(x=date,y=return,group=Company,color=Company)) + geom_line(size=0.66,na.rm=TRUE,show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, size = 1.0, color="grey70") +
  theme_gray(base_size = 24) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c( "#009E73","#E69F00","#000000", "#56B4E9"),

    labels = c("NVidia", "Meta", "Apple", "Microsoft"))  +
  theme(
    strip.background  = element_blank(),

                                          linewidth =0),
          panel.grid.minor.y = element_line(color="white",linewidth = 0.5),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color="white",linewidth = 0.5),
          panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),

title: Meetup 3: Visualization Quality Features
text:
Principle of Uniformity of Graphics

Represent data directly proportional to ink/graphics

Lie Factor = (size of effect shown in graphic) / (size of effect in data)
Proportional Ink

Clear, detailed, and thorough labeling

Write explanations on the graphic.
Label important events

Show data variation, not design variation

title: Meetup 3: Visualization Quality Features
text:
Principal of Proportional Ink

“The representation of numbers, as physically measured on the surface of the graphic itself, should be directly proportional to the numerical quantities represented.” (1983, p.56) Edward Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information


This principle avoids many misleading visualizations

title: Meetup 3: Visualization Quality Features

Scale doesn’t start at 0
Width expands with height
Danger in bar plots, filled line plots, plots with elements that scale with data

title: Module 8 - Distributions and Histograms
text:
Overview and Deliverables

10/19: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Story 4 is due at the end of this week (Sunday 10/25)

There are two primary goals for this week:

Read Chapters 7-9 in Fundamentals of Data Visualization
Finish Data Story 4 and turn it in (Sunday by midnight)


Readings

Wilke - Chapters 7-9



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 8 - Visualizing Distributions
In this meetup we go over techniques for visualizing distributions. This starts with tips and tricks to optimize your histograms, frequency-polygons, and density plots. We then move on to visualizing cumulative distribution functions and show how to generate the empirical CDF and how that leads to qq-plots. Finally, we introduce tools for working with multiple distributions, such as ridge plots.
Spring 2025 recording

title: Module 6 - Storytelling
text:
Overview and Deliverables

10/5: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Story 3 is due at the end of this week (Sunday 10/11)

The goal of this week is to learn about different narrative structures and how to incorporate these structures into your data visualizations.

Readings

Storytelling with Data - Chapter 7: Lessons in Storytelling
Wilke - Chapter 29: Telling a story and making a point



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 6 - Narrative Structures
In this meetup we describe several commonly used story arcs and apply them to data analysis and visualization. Common pitfalls that arise when trying to present data to non-data-scientist audiences are presented.
Spring 2025 recording
A sample data story is also available: Electricity and Carbon Over Time (PDF)

title: Module 4 - Plotting Associations and Time Series
text:
Overview and Deliverables

9/21: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Story 2 is due at the end of this week (Sunday 9/27)

We each have had, or will have, the experience of arriving to make a presentation or having submitted a report to discover that the materials prepared do not tell the story that the audience is prepared to “hear”. From these experiences we derive what should be a mantra of storytelling with data: “Know Your Audience and The Context of the Requested Story”.

Readings

Wilke - Chapters 12 and 13



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 4 - Visualizing Associations and Time Series
In this meetup we discuss how to improve your visualizations of scatterplots and time series. We go over how to plot two quantitative variables with differing numbers of categorical variables using colors and shapes, and when to use facets. We discuss hues and bubble plots for 3 categorical variables, and pair plots for even more combinations. Then we show how to annotate scatterplots and discuss techniques for plotting time series, including season plots and polar plots.
Spring 2025 recording

title: Module 2 - Graphical Perception Theory
text:
Overview and Deliverables

9/7: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Story 1 is due this Sunday 9/13 at midnight!

This week focuses on types of data visualizations and the tools available for generating visualizations. The objective is understanding what type of visualization to use for the types of data that you are most likely to encounter and what tools are best for each type of visualization.

Readings

Wilke - Chapter 5. This provides a good overview of which types of graphs to use for which type of data. The following chapters go into depth on each individual topic, so that you can use this book as a reference (if you need to plot amounts, go to chapter 6, distributions, chapter 7, etc.)
William Cleveland: Graphical Perception Theory. This is one of the foundational (review) papers in research on visualization. If you want to know the “why” for the advice given in this class, much of it has origin in the research of Cleveland and his group.



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 2 - Graphical Perception Theory
In this meetup we go through the basics of research on the principles behind perceptual decision making. We go through the perceptual ladder and discuss the practical implications for making visualizations.

title: Module 14 - Interactive Visualizations
text:
Overview and Deliverables

12/7: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Complete work on Story 7, which is due this weekend, Sunday 12/13 at midnight


Readings

Chapter 6 of Mastering Shiny, which covers the basics of controlling the layout of a shiny app
Exploration and Explanation in Data-Driven Storytelling (PDF), a research perspective paper on how to use interactive elements to further your data story

For those of you who want to go deeper into interactive visualizations, the most famous resources (not sure if they are universally good) are Stephen Few’s Information Dashboard Design and Wexler, Shaffer, and Cotgreave’s The Big Book of Dashboards. I think the writing on this topic is generally poor and has many gaps.


Meetup
Slides: Meetup 14 - Exploring Data with Shiny
In this meetup we continue to further learn Shiny. We discuss themes and both single and multi-page layouts. We also discuss some of the differences between static and dynamic visualizations.
Spring 2025 recording

title: Module 12 - Hierarchical Clustering
text:
Overview and Deliverables

11/16: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Continue working on Story 6, due at the end of this week (Sunday 11/22)


Readings

Wikipedia article on Hierarchical Clustering
ggdendro introduction and reference
tidyheatmaps documentation
Bioinformatics Training and Education Program Tutorial on Hierarchical Clustering
For Python: Seaborn Clustermap, scipy.cluster



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 12 - Hierarchical Clustering
In this meetup we talk about hierarchical clustering, which is an alternative to traditional clustering methods. We discuss the neighbor-joining algorithm for building trees and show how to calculate them in R and visualize them using the ggdendro package. The clustered heatmap is introduced and we show how to customize them using the tidyheatmaps package. Pros and cons of the hierarchical approach are explored.
Spring 2025 recording

title: Module 10 - Dimension Reduction and PCA
text:
Overview and Deliverables

11/2: Attend the course meetup at 8:00PM Eastern
Finish working on Story 5, due at the end of this week (Sunday 11/8)


Readings

Wilke - Section 12.3: Dimension reduction
A short visual explanation of PCA can be found here: https://setosa.io/ev/principal-component-analysis/
A very in depth mathematical tutorial (optional) can be found here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1100
There are some excellent youtube videos which focus on the technique - I like the shorter videos by Steve Brunton but ymmv



Meetup
Slides: Meetup 10 - Working With High Dimensional Data
In this meetup we talk about how to use principal component analysis to visualize patterns and structures in high dimensional datasets. We show how to choose the number of principal components using the “elbow” of the variance explained curve, how to tidy PCA models in R, how to interpret principal components, and how to visualize clusters using components.

title: Textbooks
text:
Required
This course makes use of several textbooks and other resources. I have attempted when possible to choose resources which are freely available.

Claus Wilke. Fundamentals of Data Visualization

This book is a comprehensive and highly readable guide to making visualizations that accurately reflect the data, tell a story, and look professional. It is freely available online and forms the backbone of the weekly readings. The book does not have any instructions on programming, but the github page of the book is freely available and shows you exactly how to make each visualization using ‘ggplot2’ in ‘R’.

Kieran Healy. Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction

A hands-on introduction to making visualizations with ‘ggplot2’ in ‘R’, this book was recently updated and is also an excellent introduction to data visualization that manages to cover some different ground to Wilke. It has value even if you are not using ‘R’ for the course

Nicolas Rougier. Scientific Visualization: Python + Matplotlib

This book is a guide to ‘matplotlib’ which has become the industry standard python library for making visualizations. Many easier to use packages, such as ‘seaborn’, are based on it. ‘matplotlib’ can seem complex and this book helps to demystify it and explain its design principles. Rougier also writes well about principles that make a good figure.


Other Important Texts

Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic. Storytelling with Data: A Data Visualization Guide for Business Professionals

This book teaches the fundamentals of communicating effectively with data: choosing an appropriate visual, eliminating clutter, focusing attention, and building a narrative. Unfortunately it is not freely available.

William Cleveland. The Elements of Graphing Data. Hobart Press, 1994

A classic text on graphical perception theory from one of the pioneers of statistical graphics.

Rafe Donahue. Fundamental Statistical Concepts in Presenting Data

Really nice monograph that links stats to data visualization.

title: DATA 608 - Knowledge and Visual Analytics
text: This course is about the creation of high quality data visualizations - diagrams, graphs/plots, maps, tables, and interactive applications - that tell the story or stories hidden in the underlying data. You will learn the skills, techniques, and the art of “Storytelling with Data”. You will gain the knowledge and experience necessary to source data and use the tools available to you as a data practitioner to build high quality data visualizations that tell a story, conveying the information that your audience needs to know and wants to hear. Along the way we will study the theory of graphical perception, the quality features that distinguish excellent visualizations, how to visualize associations, time series, geospatial data, distributions, models and uncertainty, and how to use unsupervised learning techniques like dimension reduction and clustering to find structure in complex datasets. The course culminates with building interactive visualizations and dashboards using Shiny.

title: ZORI Data Dictionary
text:
Variables

‘cbsa’ : ‘char’ data type. Core-Based-Statistical-Area. Ranges from 10000 to 49999
‘Region’: ‘char’ data type. Name for the metropolitan statistical area, is generally the principal city and state of the MSA (note the city may not be in the state).
‘SizeRank’: ‘dbl’ data type. Population rank of the region assigned by ‘zillow’ in descending order.
‘City’: ‘char’ data type. Name of the largest principal city in the corresponding MSA.
‘State’: ‘char’ data type. Principal state in the Metro Area (defined by ‘Zillow’)
‘date’: ‘date’ data type. Date of measurement. Measurements are published on monthly intervals.
‘zori’: ‘dbl’ data type. ‘zori’ stands for Zillow Observed Rent Index. ‘zori’ is a measure constructed by zillow in order to measure the long term rent change in different geographic areas over time. It is designed to be robust to random biases in the types of properties being listed on zillow at any given moment and also to biases in the types of buildings that rent on zillow versus the overall rental stock of a given city. The units of ‘zori’ are nominal dollars. If you want to interpret ‘zori’, it is modeled as the mean of the 35-65% percentile asking rent within a given market.

title: Data Stories
text:
The homework assignments in this class are six data stories and one project. The data stories are due every two weeks, Sunday at midnight Eastern time. The data stories involve developing a series of visualizations with the aim of communicating specific insights about a given dataset. The data stories may also have a few questions related to your visualizations and the data.
The data stories should be submitted in the form of a reproducible quarto report or presentation, accompanied with a rendered PDF file or a link to a rendered html file (do not submit html files to brightspace). You may write code for your visualizations in either ‘R’ or ‘python’.
The last story involves finding your own dataset, creating your own data story using it, and publishing this story as an interactive shiny app on ‘posit.cloud’/‘shinyapps.io’. The 6 data stories are collectively worth 80% of your grade, and the final project is worth 20%. You may resubmit your data stories one time each to receive additional/partial credit in response to suggested corrections or improvements.

title: Story 2: Can the FED Control Inflation and Maintain Full Employment?
text:
Assigned: Week 3 | Due: Sunday, September 27 at midnight Eastern | Points: 100
The Federal Reserve’s mandate from Congress is to control inflation and to maintain low unemployment. You can read about it here: Dual Mandate. These seem to be contradictory objectives - see this wikipedia article on the Phillips Curve. Another good but short news article which focuses on the specific context of recessions is here: Soft Landing.
For this story you will need to source the following data for the last 25 years:

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) (Bureau of Labor Statistics) - note that there are numerous ways to define a CPI, and you can create a custom definition on the BLS page. If you want the standard CPI it is the CPI for all Urban Consumers, or CPI-U. You can find this and other BLS datasets here: https://data.bls.gov/toppicks?survey=bls
The FED Funds Rate (FRED) (Federal Reserve Board) - This can be found here: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS
Unemployment Rate (Bureau of Labor Statistics). I recommend using the seasonally adjusted rate.

Your data visualizations should be designed to answer the question “Has the FED been able to fulfill the mandate given to it by Congress?”
Notes:

I recommend using quarto to compose your report with either R or python for the visualizations, though you may use something different if you choose.
Remember, the FED raises rates after reviewing the CPI and other data, and unemployment (layoffs) occurs after company operating costs go up.
This assignment is due at the end of week four of the semester.

text:

Degree Program: M.S. in Data Science Credits: 3 graduate credits Prerequisites: DATA 602; DATA 607 Type of Course: Required Course

Description
This course is about the creation of high quality data visualizations - diagrams, graphs/plots, maps/geographic visualizations, tables, and interactive applications - that tell the story or stories hidden in the underlying data. You will learn the skills, techniques and the art of “Storytelling with Data”. You will gain the knowledge and experience necessary to source data and use the tools available to you as a data practitioner to build high quality data visualizations that tell a story, conveying the information that your audience needs to know and wants to hear.


Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, as a data practitioner you will:

Be able to create high quality data graphics using various libraries (Python, R and/or JavaScript), web applications, and/or desktop applications.
Understand the quality factors that distinguish high quality data graphics.
Have developed a “Critical Eye”, the ability to discern poor quality and misleading data visualizations as differentiated from those of high quality.
Be cognizant of the data story process and your role as a data practitioner in identifying the story audience and the required story content, determining the context of the story, and the iterative process of developing high quality data visualizations and accompanying text.



Program Learning Outcomes addressed by the course

Business Understanding. Learn when analytical and/or probabilistic techniques apply to certain categories of business problems, and be able to build data stories that guide business decisions.
Foundational Data Visualization Skills. Explore and analyze data, build probabilistic and statistical models, and create meaningful data stories using the craft of data visualization.
Presentation. Complete and submit assignments using techniques from the course.

title: Story 1: Housing Policy and Affordability
text:
Overview
For this assignment, you are assuming the role for a data scientist working for a city government and you have been tasked with providing technical advice to the mayor and city council about whether or not permitting reform could help address housing affordability. You have access to a dataset which which provides demographic and economic information at a number of different organizational levels across the country. The assignment will consist of parts where you will answer questions about visualizations that are presented to you, and other parts where you improve upon them to make them more informative or so that they tell a better story.

title: Story 1: Housing Policy and Affordability
text:
Background
In recent years, many parts of the United States have experienced an increase in housing costs. The Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies published a report on the State of the Nation’s Housing in 2026. Amongst the 10 takeaways from that report include a major decline in residual income for renters earning under $30,000 dollars per year, record high median homeownership costs, and an increase in price of the cheapest rental units. High housing prices have been implicated as a cause of homelessness and other major problems in large metro areas, according to a report by the Pew Foundation.
Many different policies have been proposed to address this issue, including permitting reform. Recent data suggests that increased permitting slows or reverses increases in housing prices, with rent declines in fast-growing sun-belt cities such as Austin being held up as exemplars of this policy, see for example Austin’s Surge of New Housing Construction Drives Down Rents, which describes the issue in Austin primarily, and New Housing Slows Rent Growth Most for Older, More Affordable Units. However, this is still an area of active research where there is much debate about the causal factors of housing costs. If you want to learn more about the nuances here are some references:

E. Glaeser and J. Gyourko. The Economic Implications of Housing Supply. JEP (2018). 32:1
V. Been, I. Gould Ellen, and K. O’Reagan. _Supply Skepticism Revisited. Housing Policy Debate. (2025). 35.1
A. Damiano. Supply Skepticism or Supply Realism?. Housing Policy Debate. (2025). 35.1

Density

Density estimates a smooth curve from the points
Uses kernel density estimation or kde \[
p(x|{x_i}) = \frac{1}{nb_W}\sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x-x_i}{b_W}\right)
\]
\(K\) is a standard probability distribution
\(b_W\) is called the bandwidth
